blocks.text: The charge comes in two forms, and both travel widely. The first asks it as arithmetic. Your book says We created you, We sent down the Reminder, We built the heaven. A plural speaker is plural, so who are the others helping Allah? The second asks it as confusion. The same book keeps moving between We, He, and I, sometimes inside one passage, and a speaker who knows who he is does not keep changing his own pronouns.

blocks.text: Both forms assume one thing, that an Arabic pronoun counts its referents the way an English pronoun does. It does not. Arabic has a standing plural of majesty, a we that one exalted speaker says of himself alone. The rule is printed in the grammar books, alive in the poets, and used by the Quran itself for single referents of no theological weight at all. When the Quran means that others act alongside Allah, it names them. When it wants the nearness of answer, it drops the say-command and speaks as I. When it describes the Lord for the servant to learn of Him, it says He. One Speaker, and many rooms of speech.

blocks.text: The school's senior classical commentator states the rule first. The speech of one speaker can run in the plural form for greatness of station, and he says this is simply how speakers of Arabic talk. His proof text is the charge's own target, the doubled We of the Reminder verse (Qur'an 15:9), and the We of man's creation (Qur'an 23:12). The report he relays records both edges. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, a founder of Arabic grammar, was asked about the plural of the dying soul's plea in Qur'an 23:99, send them back, addressed to the one God. He declined to force a parse and said he does not know its analysis, because it is a plural, and the people of his circle found the reserve good. The reserve predates the rule, and the rule answers the reserve. The founder's own stated reason is form-side, because it is a plural, and the Kufan school answered him within a generation. That reading is exhibited below. Al-Tusi's statement is the tradition resolving what the founder left open, the plural of rank named where he paused. It runs in both directions, a creature addressing the one God in the plural and God speaking of Himself in it. Neither direction carries number.

blocks.text: Every human we on exhibit gathers rank around a speaker standing with his people, and the divine We gathers rank without needing any. The case of a speaker standing alone rests on three legs. The grammar of section 1 states the rule. The kings' custom, which al-Razi explains in section 7, shows it in use. And the verse of the two directions, Qur'an 23:99, has a creature addressing the one God in the plural inside the book itself. The grammarians wrote after the book, and the book is their largest text. The poets and the kings' custom are the usage no scripture controls. And the question of codification cuts both ways. A rule read out of the Quran would explain the Quran perfectly and nothing else. This rule explains the poets, the kings, the dying soul's plea, and the book at once, and a rule that explains all of them was already in the language. The demand for a pre-Islamic king saying we of himself alone should also be measured against the opponent's own ground. The only divine plurals his canon carries are in-scripture, Genesis 1:26 and its companions, and the only in-scripture plural-for-one the Quran needs is likewise inside the book, the dying soul's plea and the single Prophet addressed in the plural. A bar that the opponent's own evidence does not clear is not a bar the Quran has to clear.

blocks.text: The comparison runs on four named tests. First, what each view asks a believer to accept about God. Second, whether each reading coheres with its own scripture. Third, which reading fits the words themselves. Fourth, which demands less of the text.

blocks.text: On the first test, each reading must square with its own scripture's monotheism, and both books hold the pair, plural forms and strict oneness, without dissolving either. On the second, the Quranic reading is a rule of the language the book speaks, settled by dictionaries, grammars, and usage. The Trinitarian reading of Genesis reads the fourth-century creed back into Hebrew written a millennium before it.

blocks.text: On the third test, the words themselves. Augustine argues from the plural pronouns to plurality of persons, so the number of the pronoun is the load-bearing point, and the Hebrew grammar gives it no such freight. The noun of God stands under singular agreement, and Deuteronomy above shows a plural noun of God standing under one LORD, with nobody reading the morphology as a census. Genesis 1:26's verb is plural in form, like the Arabic nahnu, and English answers that case with its own royal we. The queen says we are, and never we is, one speaker under plural agreement. On the fourth test, the plural of majesty needs no extra persons and no creed to import them, while the Trinitarian reading needs Nicaea to decide what the us means.

blocks.text: The strongest remaining objection is the retinue reading. Read the king's we as executors hidden inside the pronoun, and the divine We becomes Allah with his angels as his retinue. The charge needs helpers of the divine act who share the act's rank. The book gives creatures who carry out the act of the One. **(a) Creedal form (John 1:3 / Col 1:16 beyond the four tests): closed as an escape from this article's verdict; not refuted, and honestly not claimed to be.** Section 8 already states the boundary plainly: "the four tests cannot reach his form of the case. That is sound scoping, not overreach: the page's stated thesis is the pronoun charge in its two forms ("does We mean others help Allah" and "why the shifts"), so retreating to Nicaea abandons the load-bearing premise of that charge. What remains is a different article (the creedal case on its own ground), which the page correctly says "must be argued from there." Within the declared scope, genuinely closed; no pronoun article can close it further.

**(b) Pre-Islamic attestation of a strictly solitary royal we: materially weakened, with the residual honestly conceded rather than hidden.** The al-Farra chain does three distinct things. First, it dates the rule to d. 207 AH at the founding grammatical layer, so the rule is no longer a fifth-century Shi'i harmonization meeting the reader first at al-Tusi. Second, it exhibits the rule *inside the Quran at a theologically neutral verse*: 65:1, "the singular title of honor and the plural verb in one clause," which answers the circularity objection the page itself states best ("A rule read out of the Quran would explain the Quran perfectly and nothing else," line 545). Third, al-Farra glosses the divine Our itself ("plural in form and singular in meaning") and equates the creature's plural of 23:99 with "We created you before" (20:115), so the divine-We-as-majesty reading is attested at the earliest layer in both directions. Residual, and the page concedes it: the strictly solitary pre-Islamic we is still exhibited only through post-Quranic compilation ("Every human we on exhibit gathers rank around a speaker standing with his people"), and al-Farra is still two centuries after the book. The escape now requires discounting all post-Quranic grammar, which destroys the opponent's own Arabic philology. Weakened to a tolled position, not fully closed.

**(c) al-Khalil's reserve: closed as far as dated texts allow.** The reframe rests on checkable chronology: "The reserve predates the rule, and the rule answers the reserve. The founder paused over the parse, not the referent, and his own Kufan succession answered him within a generation" (line 427). Al-Khalil d. 170 AH, al-Farra d. 207 AH through al-Kisa'i's circle; "within a generation" is accurate. The reserve is scoped by al-Khalil's own stated reason ("because it is plural"). One wording outruns the quote slightly (finding F3 below). No textual escape remains; only the skeptic who discounts the whole grammatical tradition, which is hatch (b)'s tolled position again.

**What remains overall:** the token-ambiguity objection (Seat 2) and the strictly-solitary-we concession. Both are standing residuals of evidence, not defects of inference.

## Seat 2 — Reasoning

**The al-Farra chain is multi-link, not a single generalization.** "The Arabs use the plural verb for one person" (v3 p42) alone would *not* license "the divine We carries no number"; that is a second-person address construction generalizing to first person. But the page does not rest there: the 11:37 gloss is a direct statement on the divine first-person Our ("expressed in the plural while its meaning is singular"), and the 23:99 ↔ 20:115 equation puts creature-to-God plural and God's own We under one rule in one running comment. **The 65:1 parallel holds as internal usage on al-Farra's stated reading, and that is its one dependency.** Correctly attributed ("The earliest commentary on the grammar of these verses counts no second speaker," line 466), but the mainstream alternative reading of talaqtum (the Prophet together with the community, the ruling generalized) is unengaged; on that reading the plural counts real referents and the neutral-exhibit force drops. One sentence acknowledging and weighing it would close the gap.

**The scope-catcher is an argument, not a device.** It is a dilemma: either the pronoun carries number, and then the four tests apply and "a method that convicts the Quran's We convicts Genesis first"; or it does not, and the pronoun charge fails. Retreating to the creed abandons the pronoun as load-bearing, which concedes the stated thesis. Its one unsupported premise is empirical (F5). "Deserves its own sentence" is ornament; the logic beneath it is sound.

**Strongest objection to the thesis:** grant every grammatical rule and claim residual ambiguity — ordinary-language rules license a reading without fixing reference token by token, and the creed breaks the tie. The page's counters already exist: the naming rule ("When creatures share in an act, the Quran never hides them in a pronoun," line 625) and the 6:99 one-sentence shift ("He sent down, then We brought forth... the subject unchanged," line 667). The naming rule is an inductive universal over the book, and "Different hands cannot hide inside one sentence" answers clause-level editorial seams only by assertion. The page's strongest available reply, present but never gathered into one place, is burden reversal: the charge needs the plural to carry number, and every theologically neutral token (65:1, the mosques, the callers) testifies it does not. One sentence doing that explicitly would meet the objection at full strength.

## Seat 1 — First Principles: the three hatches

**(a) Creedal form (John 1:3 / Col 1:16 beyond the four tests): closed as an escape from this article's verdict; not refuted, and honestly not claimed to be.** Section 8 already states the boundary plainly: "the four tests cannot reach his form of the case. That was the charge the polemic itself chose when it likened the Quran's We to Genesis 1:26." That is sound scoping, not overreach: the page's stated thesis is the pronoun charge in its two forms ("does We mean others help Allah" and "why the shifts"), so retreating to Nicaea abandons the load-bearing premise of that charge. What remains is a different article (the creedal case on its own ground), which the page correctly says "must be argued from there." Within the declared scope, genuinely closed; no pronoun article can close it further.

**(b) Pre-Islamic attestation of a strictly solitary royal we: materially weakened, with the residual honestly conceded rather than hidden.** The al-Farra chain does three distinct things. First, it dates the rule to d. 207 AH at the founding grammatical layer, so the rule is no longer a fifth-century Shi'i harmonization meeting the reader first at al-Tusi. Second, it exhibits the rule *inside the Quran at a theologically neutral verse*: 65:1, "the singular title of honor and the plural verb in one clause," which answers the circularity objection the page itself states best ("A rule read out of the Quran would explain the Quran perfectly and nothing else," line 545). Third, al-Farra glosses the divine Our itself ("plural in form and singular in meaning") and equates the creature's plural of 23:99 with "We created you before" (20:115), so the divine-We-as-majesty reading is attested at the earliest layer in both directions. Residual, and the page concedes it: the strictly solitary pre-Islamic we is still exhibited only through post-Quranic compilation ("Every human we on exhibit gathers rank around a speaker standing with his people"), and al-Farra is still two centuries after the book. The escape now requires discounting all post-Quranic grammar, which destroys the opponent's own Arabic philology. Weakened to a tolled position, not fully closed.

**(c) al-Khalil's reserve: closed as far as dated texts allow.** The reframe rests on checkable chronology: "The reserve predates the rule, and the rule answers the reserve. The founder paused over the parse, not the referent, and his own Kufan succession answered him within a generation" (line 427). Al-Khalil d. 170 AH, al-Farra d. 207 AH through al-Kisa'i's circle; "within a generation" is accurate. The reserve is scoped by al-Khalil's own stated reason ("because it is plural"). **What remains overall:** the token-ambiguity objection (Seat 2) and the strictly-solitary-we concession. Both are standing residuals of evidence, not defects of inference.

## Seat 2 — Reasoning

**The al-Farra chain is multi-link, not a single generalization.** "The Arabs use the plural verb for one person" (v3 p42) alone would *not* license "the divine We carries no number"; that is a second-person address construction generalizing to first person. But the page does not rest there: the 11:37 gloss is a direct statement on the divine first-person Our ("expressed in the plural while its meaning is singular"), and the 23:99 ↔ 20:115 equation puts creature-to-God plural and God's own We under one rule in one running comment. The chain holds.

**The 65:1 parallel holds as internal usage on al-Farra's stated reading, and that is its one dependency.** Correctly attributed ("The earliest commentary on the grammar of these verses counts no second speaker," line 466), but the mainstream alternative reading of talaqtum (the Prophet together with the community, the ruling generalized) is unengaged; on that reading the plural counts real referents and the neutral-exhibit force drops. One sentence acknowledging and weighing it would close the gap.

**The scope-catcher is an argument, not a device.** It is a dilemma: either the pronoun carries number, and then the four tests apply and "a method that convicts the Quran's We convicts Genesis first"; or it does not, and the pronoun charge fails. Retreating to the creed abandons the pronoun as load-bearing, which concedes the stated thesis. Its one unsupported premise is empirical (F5). "Deserves its own sentence" is ornament; the logic beneath it is sound.

**Strongest objection to the thesis:** grant every grammatical rule and claim residual ambiguity — ordinary-language rules license a reading without fixing reference token by token, and the creed breaks the tie. The page's counters already exist: the naming rule ("When creatures share in an act, the Quran never hides them in a pronoun," line 625) and the 6:99 one-sentence shift ("He sent down, then We brought forth... the subject unchanged," line 667). The naming rule is an inductive universal over the book, and "Different hands cannot hide inside one sentence" answers clause-level editorial seams only by assertion. The page's strongest available reply, present but never gathered into one place, is burden reversal: the charge needs the plural to carry number, and every theologically neutral token (65:1, the mosques, the callers) testifies it does not. One sentence doing that explicitly would meet the objection at full strength.

paragraphs.text: وفي إيراد « إياك » دون « إياه » ، كما هو مقتضى الظاهر ، التفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب . ومن النكتة الخاصة ، في الالتفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب ، في هذا المقام ، بعد اشتماله على فائدة عامة ، من جهة المتكلم ، وهي التصرف والافتنان في وجود الكلام واظهار القدرة عليها ، ومن جهة المخاطب ، وهي تطرية نشاطه في سماع الكلام ، وايقاظه للإصغاء إليه . أنه لما قيل : « إياك » بدل « إياه » ، فقد نزل الغائب بواسطة أوصافه المذكورة التي أوجب تميزه وانكشافه ، حتى صار كأنه تبدل خفاء غيبته ، بجلاء حضوره ، منزلة المخاطب في التمييز والظهور

The use of iyyaka carries the speech from referring to someone absent into directly addressing Him. This shift has a general benefit. For the speaker, it shows skill and variety in expression. For the hearer, it renews attention and wakes the listener to hear carefully. Here it has a further purpose. The word iyyaka brings the One previously spoken of through His qualities into the position of one directly addressed. Those qualities distinguished Him and made Him known. The hiddenness of His absence became as clear as His presence. He therefore became like one directly addressed in clarity and distinction.

paragraphs.text: المسألة الرابعة : إذا كان المقصود إثبات التوحيد ، فكيف قال : * ( بنيناها ) * ولم يقل بنيتها أو بناها الله ؟ نقول قوله : * ( بنينا ) * أدل على عدم الشريك في التصرف والاستبداد وقوله بنيتها يمكن أن يكون فيه تشريك ... فإذن علم أن المراد جمع التعظيم وأفاد النص عظمته ، فالعظمة أنفى للشريك فثبت أن قوله : * ( بنيناها ) * أدل على نفي الشريك من بنيتها وبناها الله . فإن قيل : لم قلت : إن الجمع يدل على التعظيم ؟ قلنا الجواب من الوجهين . الأول : أن الكلام على قدر فهم السامع ، والسامع هو الإنسان ، والإنسان يقيس الشاهد على الغائب ، فإن الكبير عندهم من يفعل الشيء بجنده وخدمه ولا يباشر بنفسه ، فيقول الملك فعلنا أي فعله عبادنا بأمرنا ويكون في ذلك تعظيم ، فكذلك في حق الغائب

Fourth question. If the aim is to establish God's oneness, why does He say, "We built it," and not, "I built it," or, "God built it"? We answer, "We built it" more clearly shows that no one shares His control or independent power. "I built it" may suggest a partnership. The intended meaning is therefore the plural of majesty. The wording shows His greatness. His greatness excludes any partner. Thus, "We built it" more clearly denies a partner than "I built it" or "God built it." If someone asks, "Why do you say that the plural shows majesty?" We answer in two ways. First, speech follows what the listener can understand. The listener is human. People compare what they see with what they cannot see. They consider great a ruler who acts through his armies and servants without acting personally. A king says, "We did it," meaning, "Our servants did it by our command." This gives him majesty. The same applies to the Unseen.

paragraphs.text: والجمع للعظمة والكبرياء وفيه من تعظيم أمر الإجابة ما فيه ؛ وأخرج ابن مردويه عن عائشة رضي اللّه تعالى عنها قالت : «كان النبي صلّى اللّه عليه وسلم إذا صلى في بيتي فمر بهذه الآية وَلَقَدْ نادانا نُوحٌ فَلَنِعْمَ الْمُجِيبُونَ قال : صدقت ربنا أنت أقرب من دعا وأقرب من بغى فنعم المدعو ونعم المعطي ونعم المسؤول ونعم المولى أنت ربنا ونعم النصير»

The plural expresses majesty and greatness, and it gives the act of answering great importance. Ibn Marduyah reported from Aisha that whenever the Prophet prayed in her home and passed this verse, "Noah called upon Us, and how excellent are We in answering," he said, "You have spoken the truth, our Lord. You are nearer than the one who calls upon You, and nearer than the one who transgresses. How excellent are You to call upon, how excellent are You to give, how excellent are You to ask, how excellent are You as Master. You are our Lord, and how excellent are You as Helper."

paragraphs.text: فالأسلوب القرآني حين يأتي ب «إني» يشير إلى وحدة الذات ، وحين يأتي ب «إنا» يشير إلى تجمع صفات الكمال ... لذلك لا بد من ضمير التعظيم الذي يقول فيه النحويون : إن «نحن» و «نا» للمعظم نفسه . وقد عظم الحق نفسه ؛ لأن الأمر هنا حشد صفات يتطلبها إيجاد الكون والقيام على أمر الكون . ... فسبحان رب فوق كل مظنة * تعالى جلالا أن يحاط بذاته / إذا قال «إني» ذاك وحدة قدسه * وإن قال «إنّا» ذاك حشد صفاته

When the Quranic style says, "I," it points to the oneness of the Divine Being. When it says, "We," it points to the gathering of perfect qualities. Therefore, the pronoun of majesty is necessary. Grammarians say that "We" and "Us" refer to the One who is great. The Truth has declared His own greatness because creating the universe and governing it require a gathering of attributes. Glory be to a Lord beyond every assumption. His majesty is too high for His Being to be fully understood. When He says, "I," that expresses the oneness of His holiness. When He says, "We," that expresses the gathering of His attributes.
